executive_summary: AUD/CAD closed at 0.98238 on Friday 30 October 2026, meaning 1 AUD buys 0.98238 CAD. The pair is down 0.35% over one month, 0.85% over three months and 0.24% over six months, but up 7.26% over one year, and it sits at the 80th percentile of its 52-week closing range (0.9086–1.0008). The main story is a contest between interest rates and terms of trade. The policy-rate gap is 210bp: RBA 4.60% against the Bank of Canada's 2.50% after its 28 October hike. It widens to 235bp if the RBA hikes to 4.85% on 3 November, and listed futures already price that. Against this, oil above USD 100 and iron ore at a two-year low are both moving the commodity balance toward Canada. Both dossiers are Neutral against the US dollar. In this cross, though, AUD's strongest positive (a hawkish RBA path) meets CAD's strongest negative (flat GDP, falling employment, core inflation of 1.8–1.9%), and the two reinforce each other. The tactical stance is therefore Bullish at conviction 2 with a weighted score of +0.165. The strategic stance is Neutral at conviction 2 with a score of −0.0172, because over six months the record Australian current-account deficit against a Canadian surplus cancels the carry advantage. One caveat should be stated up front. In October the RBA hike odds rose from about 20% to 85–88%, yet the pair slipped and printed lower highs from 1.0008 to 0.9968 to 0.9911. The tactical long should therefore be run with a defined stop: a daily close below 0.9715, about two daily ranges (ATR) below spot.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Valuation points against AUD. The BIS real effective exchange rate is 116.13 for AUD (September 2026, the highest in the G10+SGD set and up 8.77 points in a year) and 95.59 for CAD (the lowest reading since at least January 2024). That 20.54-point gap is the widest structural divergence between the two commodity blocs in the dossiers' window. On World Bank 2025 PPP conversion factors, implied fair value is about 0.834, so spot at 0.98238 is roughly 17.8% above purchasing-power parity. What is priced at 0.98 is a carry premium of 210–235bp on top of a valuation that already discounts Australian rate leadership. What is not priced is any convergence of real exchange rates toward the terms-of-trade shift. The PPP gap has no mean-reversion clock inside six months, so it works as a cap on upside ambition rather than as a timing signal.

market_context.recent_regime: October was the month CAD won the terms-of-trade argument despite AUD winning the rates argument. AUD/USD rose 1.47% and USD/CAD fell 1.79%, so CAD's broad rally was slightly larger than AUD's. By late October the Canadian dollar had rallied against all the FX majors except the Australian dollar, but the pair gave up even that edge in the final two sessions. The decisive day was 15 October: a 110-pip fall from 0.99253 to 0.98153 on the day Singapore iron ore futures hit their two-year low near USD 89.75. bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: Annualised carry is +210bp for a long AUD/CAD at the current policy rates (RBA 4.60% vs Bank of Canada 2.50%), rising to +235bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November. The annualised premium between the November and December listed futures is −237.8bp (observed 29 October); it falls wholly after 3 November, so it already embeds the post-hike gap, and by covered interest parity it combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated. Carry-to-volatility is 0.34 at 210bp and 0.38 at 235bp on the estimated three-month implied of 6.155%. Adjusted for the estimate's known downward bias (implied of 6.7–7.5%), the ratio falls to 0.28–0.35; against 60-day realised volatility of 5.19% it is 0.40–0.45. Among AUD crosses this is second only to AUD/CHF (0.652), and well above AUD/USD (about 0.10–0.12). Forward points are derived from the −237.8bp futures calendar premium on an actual/365 basis applied to the 30 October spot.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two policy rates are 210bp apart. The RBA Cash Rate Target is 4.60%, raised 25bp on 29 September on a 9-0 vote. The Bank of Canada's rate is 2.50% after its 28 October hike, its first since July 2023. The daily central-bank series still showed the Canadian rate at 2.25% on 26 October, which implies a 235bp gap, but that reading comes from before the hike and is not used here. The next scheduled move is on the Australian side. The RBA decides on 3 November, and cash-rate futures price an 85-88% chance of a hike to 4.85%, which would take the gap back to 235bp. The Bank of Canada does not decide again until 9 December, and that meeting is priced as a hold. Most of the widening is already priced. The annualised premium between the November and December AUD/CAD futures is -237.8bp, and that window falls wholly after 3 November, so it already reflects a 4.85% versus 2.50% gap. The edge therefore lies in the paths after the meetings. The AUD dossier expects hawkish RBA guidance to bring a second hike forward by a quarter. The CAD dossier judges that pricing for a Bank of Canada hike by January is about 11bp too rich after a flat August GDP print and an estimated -0.1% for September. If either error is corrected, the expected differential widens relative to what is priced. That reaches the pair through the front end: the Australian 2-year at 4.93% yields about 162bp more than the Canadian 2-year at 3.31%.

tactical.what_is_priced: The 3 November RBA hike is almost fully priced, and so is a Bank of Canada hike by January. What is left leans toward a wider gap: hawkish RBA guidance is worth more to the Australian front end than is priced, and the January Bank of Canada pricing is about 11bp richer than Canadian core inflation and activity support.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months, the level of the gap matters more than the next 25bp. Neither dossier expects it to compress much from the 235bp it reaches after 3 November. The AUD dossier puts the RBA peak at 4.85%, with a 35% chance of 5.10% by March 2027. The CAD dossier puts the Bank of Canada peak at 2.75% no earlier than March, with a 40% chance the Bank stops at 2.50%. Both markets price more tightening than their dossier expects: the RBA path is about 10-15bp too hawkish and the Bank of Canada path 15-25bp too hawkish. The Canadian overpricing is larger, so the net correction leaves a small bias in Australia's favour of roughly 5-10bp. Core inflation anchors this asymmetry. Australia's trimmed mean of 3.7% sits above the RBA's 2-3% band, while Canada's CPI-trim and CPI-median of 1.8-1.9% sit below 2%. That leaves the RBA less room to cut early than the Bank of Canada has to stop early. The main risk to the stance is the shift to a neutral bias that the AUD dossier expects from the RBA at its 9 February 2027 meeting. That shift would remove support through expectations while leaving the carry intact. Carry of 210-235bp against an estimated three-month implied volatility of 6.155% gives a carry-to-volatility ratio of 0.34-0.38, a better reward for risk than AUD earns against the US dollar.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth and inflation gap favours Australia in how each central bank is likely to react. Growth is 2.14% year on year in Australia against 0.95% in Canada. Canada's third quarter is tracking about 1.3% annualised against the Bank of Canada's 2.0% projection, after a flat August and an estimated -0.1% in September. Core inflation is 185bp apart: Australia's September-quarter trimmed mean is 3.7%, against an average of 1.85% for Canada's CPI-trim and CPI-median. Canada's case for further hikes therefore rests on headline energy prices, with gasoline up 27.8%, while Australia's inflation is broader. Both labour markets are weakening. Australian employment fell 39,300 in September and unemployment rose to 4.7%. Canadian employment fell 68,300 and unemployment is 6.5%, the larger shock relative to the size of the labour force. The data in the next four weeks come mostly from Canada first: the Labour Force Survey on 6 November, where the CAD dossier expects a third decline, and CPI on 16 November, where core is expected to stay below 2%. The market's January Bank of Canada hike is more exposed to those prints than the RBA path is to the Australian wage, labour and CPI releases later in November. Australia's own weakness keeps confidence low: an October composite PMI of 47.7 and three straight rises in unemployment.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months both economies face the same cost-push stagflation from the oil shock, and each dossier is bearish on its own currency's growth. The AUD dossier expects Australian unemployment near 4.9% by February 2027 and the trimmed mean easing to about 3.4% by the March quarter as fuel effects drop out of the annual rate. The CAD dossier expects Canadian unemployment of 6.7-6.8% by the first quarter, growth near 1.5% in 2027 and core inflation below 2.2%. The gap between the two is therefore stable rather than widening. Australia keeps the faster growth and the higher core inflation. Canada keeps the weaker labour market and the below-target core. The cycles differ in one way that matters for the pair. Australia's inflation forces the RBA to hold a restrictive rate into a slowdown, which supports carry but erodes growth. Canada's below-target core lets the Bank of Canada stop early, which removes rate support but cushions growth. Real wages are falling in Australia, with wage growth of 3.2% against 4.3% CPI. Canadian hourly wages are up only 2.3%, so neither economy shows a wage-price spiral. On a one-to-six-month view these effects roughly cancel, so the factor scores zero.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: AUD is the more sensitive of the two legs to risk appetite. It is the G10's highest-beta currency to equities and to China. CAD is anchored by its link to the US economy, and the CAD dossier finds it outperforms AUD, NZD and NOK in risk-off phases. That makes AUD/CAD a moderately risk-sensitive pair, and the current mix leans against it. Credit is flashing a warning beneath a mid-range VIX of 17.2: US investment-grade spreads of 89bp and high-yield spreads of 326bp are at the 96th and 95th percentiles of their one-year ranges. China's October manufacturing PMI fell to 49.3 from 50.1. That hits the Australian leg directly through iron ore demand and leaves the Canadian leg largely untouched. Oil adds a twist specific to this pair. Brent above USD 110 on Hormuz disruption is a negative growth shock for Asia, where Australia sells, and a windfall for Canada. A supply-driven oil shock therefore acts like risk-off for AUD/CAD even when equities hold up. The AUD dossier puts a credit-led sell-off within four weeks at 20-30%, and it would hurt AUD more than CAD.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the risk regime cuts both ways for AUD/CAD. The bearish branch is a credit-led slowdown or a pullback in AI spending that pushes high-yield spreads above 400bp. AUD's higher beta and hedge rebalancing by Australian super funds would then weigh on the pair. The bullish branch has two parts. A Hormuz settlement would lift Asian growth and Chinese demand while removing Canada's oil windfall. A dovish Fed repricing after the midterms would weaken the dollar, as BBH's study of past midterms suggests, and both dossiers expect AUD to gain more than CAD in that case. China's third-quarter GDP beat at 4.5% year on year and possible support from the December Central Economic Work Conference are modest offsets for the Australian leg. Each dossier gives the risk-off and risk-on tails roughly equal odds, with range-bound risk appetite as the central case. With balanced tails and no sign of a regime shift, the factor carries no directional weight over six months.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: CFTC data for the week to 27 October show speculators short both legs, which mutes the signal for the pair, but the two shorts differ in quality. On the AUD side, the legacy non-commercial net short is 128,300 contracts, beyond the -80,000 level that has historically marked AUD extremes. Asset managers are net short 125,237, the second-largest short in the 25 weeks since May, and the latest week brought their first reduction since September. On the CAD side, leveraged funds are short 96,747 contracts and still adding. Asset managers, however, have covered from -108,343 in July to -1,325, and the legacy net short has narrowed to 66,400, inside the -80,000 CAD extreme. The AUD short is therefore the more crowded and more driven by real money, while the CAD short is mostly fast money funded by carry. Options on the legs agree. One-month AUD/USD 25-delta risk reversals are -0.885 vols with puts bid, while USD/CAD skew is flat at +0.013 vols. Downside protection on AUD is already well owned, and none is held on CAD. Positioning for the pair is inferred from the two legs against the US dollar. A near-certain RBA hike meeting an extreme AUD short makes a squeeze that lifts the pair more likely. The partial offset is the leveraged CAD short, which would cover on any positive Canadian surprise.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months positioning is a smaller but still positive input. The AUD asset-manager short, worth about USD 8.8bn and roughly 39% of open interest, was built as iron ore fell and Australia's current account deficit hit a record. The AUD dossier notes that shorts built on terms of trade were held for two to three quarters in 2015 and 2019, so this one can persist. Even so, for the AUD leg to keep falling the market needs new sellers, and asset managers are already near their 25-week extreme. On the CAD side, there is no crowded real-money position on either side to unwind. Asset managers are flat, and dealers are net long 95,809, so further CAD support requires real money to go net long, which it last was in May. Cross-border flows into Canada are volatile: C$100.6bn of foreign buying of Canadian securities in the second quarter was followed by C$17.31bn of net selling in August. Japanese real-money demand for Australian bonds is a slow-moving support for AUD that does not show up in CFTC data. On balance, positioning limits the pair's downside more than it creates upside.

tactical.unwind_trigger: AUD covering is triggered by hawkish RBA guidance on 3 November that pulls a second hike into early-2027 pricing, or by a weak Canadian Labour Force Survey on 6 November that cuts Bank of Canada January pricing. Both lift the pair. The opposite trigger is a strong Canadian employment print or a US-Canada steel and auto tariff deal, which would force the leveraged CAD short to cover and push the pair down.

tactical.contrarian_case: The crowd is short AUD because of iron ore near USD 90 and a record current account deficit. On fundamentals that is right, but it is already expressed in the most crowded short in the AUD futures book. Meanwhile the RBA is about to deliver a fifth hike and is likely to keep a tightening bias. CAD's real-money shorts have already been closed, so a positive surprise for AUD meets little CAD selling to absorb it. The pair would move further than its fundamentals alone justify.

strategic.contrarian_case: A strategic short in AUD/CAD needs new AUD sellers, and the pool is nearly spent: asset managers are near their 25-week extreme and leveraged funds are only modestly long. tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the pair's defining factor, and every part of it currently runs against AUD. The shift in relative terms of trade is unusually clean. NYMEX WTI rose 14.1% in October to USD 102.00, and Brent settled at USD 113.88 on 27 October on Hormuz disruption. That is a windfall for Canada as a major crude producer and a higher fuel-import bill for Australia. Meanwhile Singapore iron ore futures were near USD 90.60 a tonne after a two-year low near USD 89.75 on 15 October. The external accounts have diverged to match. Australia's June-quarter current account deficit was a record A$27.2bn, or 3.67% of GDP. Canada's swung to a C$8.84bn surplus, about 1.03% of GDP and the first surplus since 2022. Canada's August merchandise surplus of C$4.2bn beat consensus by C$2.7bn, while Australia's August goods surplus was only A$0.495bn. Canada keeps less of the oil price than headline WTI suggests, because Western Canada Select trades USD 27 under WTI with pipelines full, and the 50% US tariff on C$20bn of Canadian goods weighs on non-energy exports. Direct bilateral trade is too small to matter. In 2024 Australia exported USD 2.1bn of goods to Canada and imported USD 2.7bn, a deficit of USD 0.6bn and well under 1% of either country's goods trade. The September trade releases on 4 November for Canada and 5 November for Australia should confirm the divergence.

The market prices its guidance almost exactly, while the CAD dossier judges the Bank's January path overpriced relative to core inflation below 2%.

External Balance takes back -0.062 at its raised 0.10 weight, Risk Appetite -0.052 and USD Liquidity -0.035, leaving a net score of +0.165, Bullish by rule. Bilaterally, AUD's strongest positive (the RBA rate path) meets CAD's strongest negative (stalling growth and core inflation below 2%), so two views that cancelled against the dollar reinforce each other in AUD/CAD. The conflict is the commodities. Oil up 14% in October and iron ore at a two-year low both favour Canada, and this pair is where the AUD dossier's case for selling AUD/CAD collides with the CAD dossier's case for buying it. What is priced is already substantial. The futures calendar spread embeds a 235bp gap after the 3 November RBA hike, so the edge is narrower: RBA guidance that pulls a second hike forward, against January Bank of Canada pricing about 11bp richer than Canadian data justify. The path of least resistance is a modest drift higher, earned partly through carry of about 19 pips a month after the expected hike, with risk concentrated in the first week. The dated catalysts are the RBA decision and US midterms on 3 November, Canadian trade on 4 November, Australian trade and the Canadian budget on 5 November, the Canadian Labour Force Survey on 6 November, Canadian CPI on 16 November, Australian wages on 18 November and Australian CPI on 25 November. Conviction is 2, not higher. The score clears the threshold only modestly, the two positive drivers are partly priced, and the external drag is the factor most likely to dominate as the horizon lengthens. Conviction is not lower because the extreme AUD short makes the pair's response to a hawkish RBA larger than its response to a dovish one. The view would be wrong if a firm Canadian employment print coincided with an RBA hike framed as the last.

tactical.path_expectation: The path has two steps, both in the first week. On 3 November the RBA decision and US midterms set the first move. With the hike largely priced, the reaction depends on the forecast table. A hawkish statement should lift the pair through the 0.9877–0.9911 band (100-day 0.9879, 28 October high 0.99109) within one to two sessions. On 6 November the Canadian Labour Force Survey either extends that move toward 0.9935–0.9960 or caps it. A move of 80–110 pips on the day is plausible; the 15 October session moved 110 pips. After that, realised volatility should settle back toward 5–6% and the pair should grind sideways to higher, helped by 19 pips a month of carry. Pullbacks should hold the 0.9800–0.9802 area (the 200-day and the 30 October low). The shape is a step up and a plateau below 0.9960, not a trend. A daily close back below 0.9800 after the RBA meeting would signal that the terms-of-trade drag is overriding the rate story again. Trade plan: entry 0.9800–0.9825 (spot down to the 200-day); stop on a daily close below 0.9715, which is 109 pips from spot, about 2 ATR and below the 2026 low; targets T1 0.9907 (+83 pips), T2 0.9960 (+136), stretch 1.0000 (+176). At conviction 2 use half a standard risk unit, sized so that a 1.1% adverse move uses only that half-unit; for example, a 25bp-of-capital risk budget with a 109-pip stop implies notional of about 23% of capital. With 20-day realised volatility at 6.08%, one daily standard deviation is about 38 pips.

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: +86 pips (+0.88%) to 0.9910, plus about 19 pips of carry over four weeks, so +105 pips in total for a long (upside case: +176 pips / +1.79% to 1.0000, plus carry)
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: −104 pips (−1.06%) to 0.9720, partly offset by carry, so about −85 pips net
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 0.83:1 on base versus downside spot, 1.24:1 including carry, and 1.69:1 on the tails (+176 vs −104)
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: Modestly favourable. The upside tail is larger because of the extreme AUD short, and carry pays to wait. However, the base payoff is smaller than the downside loss, so the edge depends on the probabilities holding, which is why conviction stays at 2.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of -0.0172 is Neutral. It reflects two substantial forces cancelling, not a lack of evidence. Policy & Rates (+0.1248) and Positioning (+0.030) are almost exactly offset by External Balance (-0.132, the largest single contribution at the raised 0.20 weight) and USD Liquidity (-0.040). Six factors score zero.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights External Balance rises to 0.20 and Guidance to 0.12, so the slow structural factors carry as much weight as rates. The result is a near-perfect standoff at -0.0172. Policy & Rates contributes +0.125, because the 225-235bp gap both dossiers expect to hold through March 2027 is a carry advantage, with a carry-to-volatility ratio of 0.34-0.38. External Balance contributes -0.132: a record Australian current account deficit against a Canadian surplus, iron ore near a two-year low against oil above USD 100, and Australia's real exchange rate near its high while Canada's is near its low. Against the dollar, the AUD dossier leaned bearish (-0.029) on terms of trade and the CAD dossier was Bearish CAD (-0.122) on its rate path. In this pair those two readings meet head on and cancel. What is priced is a second RBA hike by mid-2027 and a Bank of Canada peak at 2.75% by January. The dossiers judge both too hawkish, the Canadian path more so. That keeps the differential intact, but not enough to outweigh the external drag. The path of least resistance is carry accrual with event-driven risk in both directions, not a structural drift either way. The dated catalysts are Canadian third-quarter GDP on 30 November, the Australian balance of payments on 1 December, Australian GDP on 2 December, the back-to-back RBA and Bank of Canada decisions on 8 and 9 December, the 1 January 2027 US tariff deadline and the RBA meeting on 9 February 2027. Conviction is 2 because the score is near zero yet both drivers are strong, so the distribution has fat tails in both directions. A Hormuz settlement or a US tariff escalation on Canada would lift the pair. Iron ore below USD 85 or a dovish RBA pivot on 9 February would push it down.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically AUD ranks 7th and CAD 8th of 11 in their dossiers, so neither currency stands out and a Neutral cross fits the cross-section. Among AUD crosses, AUD/NOK is the cleaner strategic expression of the terms-of-trade drag and AUD/CHF the cleaner carry long. AUD/CAD sits between them because it carries both themes at once. Among CAD crosses, short CAD against NOK isolates relative oil exposure without the AUD terms-of-trade loss, so AUD/CAD ranks behind it as a CAD short.

strategic.path_expectation: The path should start with event-driven trading in a 0.9720–1.0010 range through December. The November catalysts and the 8–9 December back-to-back decisions set the level of the policy gap, while the 1 December Australian balance of payments sets the tone for terms of trade. The 1 January 2027 tariff deadline is a binary event for the CAD leg that could produce a 100–150 pip gap in either direction. From mid-January, the 27 January Australian CPI and the 9 February RBA meeting decide whether the expectations support for AUD fades. Our base case is a slow drift toward 0.9750–0.9800 by March–April, partly offset by carry, with rallies toward the 0.9907–0.99612 resistance zone sold. Realised volatility should rise from about 5% toward the 6.7% that six-month options imply. That would make the range wider than in 2026 but not a trend.

risk_reward.base_case_payoff: −54 pips (−0.55%) in spot; with about 115 pips of carry, a long nets about +61 pips (upside case: +326 pips / +3.32% to 1.0150, about +441 pips with carry)
risk_reward.downside_case_loss: −324 pips (−3.30%) to 0.9500, about −209 pips net of carry
risk_reward.risk_reward_ratio: 1.01:1 on the spot tails; about 2.1:1 including carry
risk_reward.asymmetry_assessment: Symmetric in spot. The only edge is carry, which is why the direction is Neutral even though a carry-funded long has slightly positive expectancy. That expectancy is too small relative to the ±325-pip tails to justify a strategic position.

consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast: Aggregated bank research puts AUD/CAD at 0.99 for Q4 2026 and 0.98 for Q1 2027 (about 0.8% above the 30 October spot by year-end and roughly back to spot by March). The same aggregation projects 0.99000 by December 2026, 0.98000 by March 2027 and 0.97260 by June 2027. Separately, UBS was reported in early August as recommending a tactical AUD/CAD long on RBA-versus-Bank of Canada policy divergence. No single bank's dated pair forecast from October was found.
consensus_divergence.bank_consensus_forecast_source: ExchangeRates.org.uk aggregation of bank research from three unnamed providers; UBS (reported early August 2026 tactical long recommendation). Model-generated forecast sites were disregarded.
consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Bullish at conviction 2. The pair should rise over four weeks as the RBA hikes and guides hawkishly while Canadian data undercut January Bank of Canada pricing.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Neutral at conviction 2. The carry advantage is offset by a relative terms-of-trade and valuation drag over one to six months.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: In line with consensus on direction for year-end. Slightly more balanced than consensus into Q1 2027, which drifts the pair back toward spot.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Small. We agree on modest AUD/CAD upside into year-end and broadly agree with the flattening into early 2027. In level terms, our tactical base case of 0.9910 sits at the aggregated year-end 0.99, and our six-month 0.9770 sits between the aggregated March (0.98) and June (0.9726) points.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: The aggregated consensus reads like a rate-divergence call, much like UBS's reported reasoning, and so do we tactically. Strategically we put more weight on relative terms of trade than consensus appears to. The Australian current account deficit is a record while Canada's is in surplus, iron ore is near a two-year low while oil is above USD 100, and Australia's real exchange rate is about 20 points above Canada's. We therefore expect the carry advantage to be absorbed rather than compounded after the RBA's likely move to a neutral bias on 9 February 2027. We also weight the 1 January 2027 US tariff decision as a two-way CAD risk that consensus does not mention.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: Tactically, a long earns the expected rise plus about 17-19 pips a month of carry. Strategically, staying Neutral avoids a long position into an external drag that the dossiers expect to build through the December balance-of-payments releases.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the external drag dominates sooner, through iron ore below USD 85 or a dovish RBA statement on 3 November, the tactical long gives back its carry and more. If a Hormuz settlement or a US tariff escalation on Canada arrives, the strategic Neutral misses a move higher in the pair. Reservations on the tactical call (published, not changing the scored stance): (1) October price action: the pair already failed to respond to a large RBA repricing; hike odds went from about 20% to 85–88% during October, yet AUD/CAD fell 0.35% and printed lower highs. (2) Canadian rates are moving against the thesis: the CAD-US 2-year differential narrowed from −160.4bp to −125.7bp in three weeks, and a growing number of big-bank economists now expect two more Bank of Canada hikes, which challenges the view that January Bank of Canada pricing is too rich. (3) The RBA hike is not fully priced in every measure: one pre-meeting survey of ASX cash-rate futures showed 78% pricing for a November hike, below the 85–88% quoted in the AUD dossier, so a hike still has some room to surprise, but a hold would be a larger shock than the dossier figures imply. The stop at 0.9715 exists because of these three points.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The difference is mechanical. Tactically, the RBA's 3 November meeting, the front-loaded Canadian data and an extreme AUD short dominate, and External Balance carries only 0.10. Strategically, External Balance rises to 0.20 and contributes -0.132. Inflation & Growth falls from 0.18 to 0.10 and turns Neutral, and Guidance turns Neutral as the RBA is expected to soften its bias. The carry advantage persists on both horizons, but over six months it is matched by the relative terms-of-trade drag.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The back-to-back RBA and Bank of Canada decisions on 8 and 9 December, followed by the RBA's 9 February 2027 meeting, where the AUD dossier expects a shift to a neutral bias. The 1 December Australian balance of payments is the main data input before them.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the Bullish view as a tactical position that earns carry around the November catalysts rather than a structural long. Reassess around the December decisions, and lean away from new longs if the Australian balance of payments confirms a wider deficit and iron ore stays below USD 90. In level terms, take profit on the tactical long into 0.9907–0.9960, the only computed resistance zone, rather than holding for parity, unless the conditions for conviction 3 are met. Treat a daily close back below the 200-day at 0.98007 after early December as the signal that the strategic drag has taken over.

forward_vs_spot.edge_3m: +84 pips above the forward. The one-month expectation of 0.9885 (0.5 × 0.9910 + 0.25 × 1.0000 + 0.25 × 0.9720) sits 80 pips above the one-month forward: about 61 pips of expected spot gain plus 19 pips of carry, the clearest edge in the report.
forward_vs_spot.edge_6m: +63 pips above the forward; our expected spot sits 54 pips below today's spot, so the strategic edge for a forward long is entirely carry, not direction, consistent with the Neutral strategic stance. A short must see the pair below 0.9707 by April just to break even.

catalysts.rationale: Cash-rate futures price 85–88% for a hike to 4.85%, which would widen the AUD-CAD policy gap from 210bp to 235bp. Futures already embed most of that, so the edge is the guidance. The November Statement on Monetary Policy is also likely to contain upgrades to inflation and the cash-rate track. That would meet an extreme AUD short while the Bank of Canada is silent until 9 December.

BBH's base case of a Democratic House and a Republican Senate tilts toward a dovish Fed repricing and a weaker dollar, which helps the higher-beta AUD leg more than CAD. A clean Republican hold would support the dollar and leave the pair driven by the RBA outcome the same day.

This is the first full month of WTI above USD 90, and the CAD dossier expects the surplus to stay above C$3bn after August's C$4.2bn. That would confirm Canada's terms-of-trade windfall, the core of the external drag on the pair.

catalysts.event: ABS international trade, September; Canadian federal budget
catalysts.rationale: The AUD dossier expects an Australian goods surplus below A$2bn, which would widen the external gap with Canada. The Canadian budget's central deficit path of about C$65bn is known, so it moves the pair only if the deficit exceeds C$75bn or a fiscal anchor is breached.

A third consecutive employment decline, with unemployment at 6.6%, would cut January Bank of Canada pricing and support the pair. A firm print would force leveraged CAD shorts to cover and is the main tactical risk; it falls on the same day as US payrolls.
CPI-trim and CPI-median at 1.8–2.0% would stand far below Australia's 3.7% trimmed mean and weaken the case for a second Bank of Canada hike, keeping the differential intact.

catalysts.event: ABS Wage Price Index, September quarter
catalysts.rationale: The expected 0.8% q/q (3.2–3.3% y/y) is consistent with falling real wages. A 1.0% q/q print would revive a second RBA hike and lift the pair through a wider expected differential.
A trimmed mean at 3.8% or higher would make the 8 December RBA meeting live and lift the pair. A reading at 3.4% or lower would cement a 4.85% peak and narrow the expected gap with Canada.

catalysts.event: Canadian GDP, third quarter and September
catalysts.rationale: Growth near 1.3% annualised against the Bank of Canada's 2.0% would confirm the growth shortfall just before the 9 December decision, weakening the case for the January hike and supporting the pair through a wider expected rate gap.

catalysts.event: ABS Balance of Payments, September quarter
catalysts.rationale: A deficit above A$28bn, another record after June's A$27.2bn, set against Canada's C$8.84bn surplus, would confirm the external divergence that dominates the strategic view and works against the carry advantage over one to six months.
The expected 0.2–0.3% q/q would narrow Australia's growth lead over Canada (2.14% vs 0.95% y/y) and strengthen the case for an RBA peak at 4.85%, eroding the growth gap that supports the rate story.

A hold at 4.85% is expected and priced. Its importance is sequence: the RBA's bias sets the tone the day before the Bank of Canada decides, and any early sign of a neutral bias would foreshadow the 9 February pivot the AUD dossier expects.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision (FOMC the same day)
catalysts.rationale: A hold with softer guidance would push the January hike out and favour the pair. A surprise hike would narrow the gap to 210bp. It is the only Bank of Canada decision on the published schedule before 1 March.

catalysts.event: Threatened increase of US tariffs on Canadian steel and cars to 50%
catalysts.rationale: Escalation (25%) would hit Canadian non-energy exports with no effect on Australia, lifting the pair. A targeted deal (35%) would release part of CAD's tariff discount and push the pair down.

The expected hold at 4.85% with a shift to a neutral bias would remove the market's mid-2027 second hike and the expectations support for AUD/CAD, while leaving carry intact. It is the strategic turning point.

assumptions: Price series: daily closing prices for AUD/CAD covering 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30. Spot is 0.98238 at the 30 October close, the last trading session before the 1 November 2026 valuation date, which falls on a Sunday. The gap is a weekend only, and every level, pip distance and percentage in the report is computed against that spot.

Moving averages and zones: computed over the full stored daily history of 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30 (1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars). The moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days. Performance figures (1M −0.35%, 3M −0.85%, 6M −0.24%, 1Y +7.26%) are as supplied with the series.

Resistance shortfall: only one resistance zone and nine support zones met the two-touch threshold. The resistance list is supplemented with the 52-week high (1.00137 intraday, 1.0008 close), parity and 1.0100. A near-term band read from the daily bars (0.9877–0.9911) is identified as such and is not a computed zone.

Policy rates: the Bank of Canada rate is taken as 2.50% from the 28 October hike. The central-bank policy-rate series still showed 2.25% on 26 October, implying a 235bp differential, but that predates the hike. The live gap is 210bp, rising to 235bp if the RBA hikes on 3 November.
Yields: the monthly 10-year yields for both countries are dated 1 September 2026 (5.283% and 3.8825%) and are not quoted as live. The 30 October daily readings (5.137% and 3.799%) are used instead.

Implied volatility: AUD/CAD implied volatility is an estimate, not a quote, built from listed AUD and CAD futures options through a realised correlation of 0.5314. The values are 5.862% at 35.7 days, 6.155% at 98.7 days and 6.657% at 189.6 days, observed 29 October. The method has run 9–18% low against directly quoted crosses and is treated as a floor. No implied-volatility percentile history exists for the cross.

Forward points: derived from the −237.8bp annualised premium between the November and December listed futures (observed 29 October), which combines the interest differential and the cross-currency basis.
Bilateral trade: IMF DOTS 2024 goods data. Australian-reported exports to Canada are USD 2.1bn and imports USD 2.7bn (net −USD 0.6bn); Canadian-reported flows are USD 2.3bn each way.

Positioning: inferred from CFTC data on the two US dollar legs for the week to 27 October 2026. Leg skews are CME-derived values that the dossiers flag as not confirmed at a public quoted source. CFTC percentile ranks and an implied-volatility percentile were not given in the report and are left null.
Scenario probabilities: the 50/25/25 split follows the framework convention. Tail-event probabilities (Hormuz, tariffs, Fed) are the dossiers' estimates.
Weights: adjusted for External Balance (+0.04) and USD Liquidity (−0.04) on both horizons, for the reasons given in the Weight Adjustments table.
Bank consensus: comes from an aggregator of three unnamed providers. Model-generated forecast sites were disregarded.
